title: Textures at the Table
description: Describe familiar food textures through clear words for how a bite feels rather than how it tastes.
cardDescription: Describe familiar food textures through clear words for how a bite feels rather than how it tastes.
focus: Texture and flavor are different qualities. These clues use common food examples to separate smoothness, firmness, moisture, and the sounds associated with a bite.
solvingTip: Look at the example and the physical quality together. Words about sweetness or seasoning would answer a different kind of clue.
words: Making repeated brittle breaking sounds when chewed, like granola
Having a rich smooth consistency like a thick custard
Separating into thin layers, as a well-made pastry can
Easy to bite or cut, rather than tough
Requiring repeated jaw movement before swallowing, like a firm caramel
Firm and breaking cleanly, as a fresh celery stalk
Free of lumps or graininess, as a well-blended sauce
Containing plenty of liquid that is released in a bite
Having a dense consistency, as a concentrated soup
Runny rather than dense, as a diluted sauce
Yielding readily to light pressure, as a ripe peach
Holding its shape under light pressure, as a set custard
Containing uneven clumps, as an incompletely mixed batter
Tending to cling to fingers, as a tacky glaze

answerNotes.CRUNCHY: Crunchy describes the texture and sound of breaking food. It is different from a flavor such as sweet or salty.
answerNotes.CREAMY: Creamy can describe a texture even when a food contains no dairy cream. The clue asks about consistency.
answerNotes.FLAKY: Flaky describes layers that separate. It is different from a uniformly smooth or chewy texture.
answerNotes.TENDER: Tender concerns how readily a food yields. It does not by itself identify how moist or strongly flavored the food is.
answerNotes.CHEWY: Chewy emphasizes resistance during chewing. It contrasts with a brittle food that breaks quickly.

title: Ways to Prepare Vegetables
description: Match common preparation verbs with the different shapes and actions used at a kitchen counter.
cardDescription: Match common preparation verbs with the different shapes and actions used at a kitchen counter.
focus: Cutting vegetables into slices, small cubes, or very fine pieces produces different results. The clues also separate removing an outer layer from removing a central portion.
solvingTip: Pay attention to the resulting size and shape. A verb describing an action is different from the name of the piece it creates.
words: To cut a vegetable into very fine pieces
To cut food into small roughly equal cubes
To cut food into broad thin pieces
To rub food against a rough perforated surface to make small shreds
To remove the central seed-bearing section of a pepper or similar produce
To cut vegetables into pieces with repeated downward strokes
To remove a vegetable's outer skin
To cut food into long narrow strips
To pass clean water over the surface of produce
To cut away unwanted ends or edges
Three-dimensional block shape made by dicing
To clean the surface of a vegetable with water
To remove the small reproductive structures from a pepper
To crush a cooked vegetable into a soft mass

answerNotes.MINCE: Mincing produces smaller pieces than ordinary chopping. The exact size depends on the preparation rather than one universal measurement.
answerNotes.DICE: Dice is a verb in this clue. Cube elsewhere in the scene names the three-dimensional shape of one piece.
answerNotes.SLICE: A slice is broad and relatively thin. It differs from a small cube made by dicing.
answerNotes.GRATE: Grating uses a toothed or perforated surface. It differs from cutting with a single smooth blade.
answerNotes.CORE: Core is an action here. It can also be a noun naming the central part being removed.

title: A Little Kitchen Chemistry
description: Explore ordinary ingredients and changes of state through direct definitions found in everyday cooking.
cardDescription: Explore ordinary ingredients and changes of state through direct definitions found in everyday cooking.
focus: This scene names physical properties and familiar ingredients without giving a recipe. Melting, freezing, and dissolving describe different changes even when they all occur in a kitchen.
solvingTip: Separate a substance from a process. Ask whether the clue describes a gas, a structure, or an action happening to an ingredient.
words: Form a solution in liquid, as sugar does in tea
Tiny living organism that helps bread dough rise
Protein network developed when wheat flour is mixed with water and worked
Plant carbohydrate used to thicken many sauces
Everyday seasoning often paired with pepper
Sweet crystalline ingredient that dissolves in tea
Chemical type found in vinegar and lemon juice
Mass of gas bubbles dispersed in a liquid or soft mixture
Jelly-like substance that holds its shape
To change from solid to liquid, as butter does when warmed
To change a liquid into a solid by cooling
To form vapor bubbles throughout a heated liquid

answerNotes.DISSOLVE: Dissolving is different from melting. Sugar can disperse in water without first turning into a pure liquid.
answerNotes.YEAST: Baker's yeast produces gas during fermentation. It is a living fungus rather than another name for baking soda.
answerNotes.GLUTEN: Gluten contributes structure to wheat dough. The term names a protein network, not a starch or a raising agent.
answerNotes.STARCH: Starch behaves differently from sugar in a mixture. Heating it with water can produce thickening through gelatinization.
answerNotes.STEAM: Water vapor itself is invisible. The visible white cloud around a kettle contains tiny condensed liquid droplets.

title: The Spice Grinder
description: Find the words for grinding tools, particle sizes, and the aromatic ingredients stored nearby.
cardDescription: Find the words for grinding tools, particle sizes, and the aromatic ingredients stored nearby.
focus: The bowl and the pounding tool of a traditional grinding set have separate names. Other clues describe the texture of the result rather than a particular spice or recipe.
solvingTip: Read whether the clue asks for a tool, an action, or a particle size. Fine and coarse describe opposite ends of the same comparison.
words: Heavy bowl in which spices are pounded
Rounded hand tool used to pound ingredients in a heavy bowl
Made up of relatively large particles after grinding
Made up of very small particles, as a powdery grind
Noticeable fragrance released by freshly ground spices
Device that reduces whole spices to smaller particles
Dry material reduced to very small loose particles
Unground, as spices sold before crushing
To break an ingredient into smaller pieces by pressure
To reduce particles by rubbing or mechanical crushing
Plant reproductive structure used as a spice in coriander
Container used to store a ground spice
Removable cover keeping a spice container closed

answerNotes.MORTAR: The mortar holds the ingredients. The pestle is the hand-held pounding or grinding tool used inside it.
answerNotes.PESTLE: The pestle is the moving tool. Its name is paired with mortar, the bowl supporting the ingredients.
answerNotes.COARSE: Coarse describes particle size rather than flavor strength. A coarse grind can still have a strong aroma.
answerNotes.FINE: Fine is relative to the intended preparation. It contrasts with coarse rather than identifying a specific spice.
answerNotes.AROMA: Aroma concerns smell. It is different from texture, which describes the physical feel of the particles.

title: Reading a Kitchen Measuring Cup
description: Use a familiar measuring cup to find words for pouring, amounts, and the cup's parts.
cardDescription: Use a familiar measuring cup to find words for pouring, amounts, and the cup's parts.
focus: The marked lines show different amounts. A spout helps pour, and the handle gives a place to hold the cup.
solvingTip: Start with a cup part or a familiar drink.
words: Kitchen vessel with marked lines for measuring liquids
Shaped lip from which liquid pours
Part of the measuring cup held in the hand
U.S. liquid measure equal to four cups
U.S. liquid measure equal to two cups
Tip the measuring cup to let liquid flow out
Mark on the cup showing a particular amount
Clear liquid often measured for a recipe
Dairy drink poured into the marked cup for baking
Containing as much liquid as the cup is meant to hold
One of two equal parts of a measured amount
Metric liquid measure printed on some measuring cups
Easy to see through, as a glass measuring cup is
Flat and even, as the surface beneath the measuring cup should be

answerNotes.CUP: Cup names the vessel here; it can also be a unit of volume.
answerNotes.SPOUT: A spout helps direct a stream out of the measuring cup.
answerNotes.HANDLE: The handle provides a grip beside the body of the cup.
answerNotes.QUART: A U.S. liquid quart contains two pints or four cups.
answerNotes.PINT: A U.S. liquid pint is half a quart.
